distant object is first diverged by the concave lens and then
converged by the eye-lens. The power of concave lens is chosen
such that it creates only that much divergence so that after the
converging action of eye-lens the image is formed on the retina.

CATARACT
The eye lens is made up of proteins arranged in a regular pattern. Because
of this regular arrangement the eye-lens is transparent. In some eyes,
the regular pattern gets disturbed and this decreases the transparency
of the eye-lens. If the arrangement disturbs to a greater extent it may
lead to an opaque eye-lens. This is called cataract. This defect is usually
found in old age.
Correction: This defect cannot be corrected by placing a suitable lens
before the eye-lens. Instead, it is corrected by a surgical operation by
replacing the affected lens by an artificial lens.
EYE DONATION
You must have seen advertisment in media persuading for eye
donation. If cornea of the eyes are removed within 6 hours of the death
of a person, it can be transplanted to a person suffering from corneal
blindness. There are more than 45 lakh cases of corneal blindness and
unfortunately out of these a major portion is that of children aged
below 2 years. If a person comes forward for eye donation, he can
save two corneal blind people by donating one eye to each. What one
has to do is go to an eye-bank, fill up the form giving his/her consent
for eye donation. On his/her death, the eye-bank is informed. Persons
from the eye-bank will come home (or in hospital) and remove the
cornea. It takes l0-5 minutes for the removal. The eye taken by the
eye-bank is checked thoroughly for any defect. If found defective it is
Persons who wear spectacles can donate eyes. Even persons having
hypertension, diabetes, etc. can donate eyes. Age is not a bar for eye
donation. But persons who are infected by AIDS, Hepatities B or C,
rabies, acute leukaemia, encephalitis, tetanus cannot donate eyes.
An eye-bank has strict standards to keep the identities of the donor
and recipient confidential. How exciting it feels to think that after one’s
death, she (or he) can make two blind persons see this wonderful world!

When the intensity of light entering the eye is high, the pupil
contracts so as to reduce the amount of light entering the eye
and vice-versa. The pupil takes some time to adjust its size. You
must have experienced that while entering a cinema hall, it is
difficult to locate your seat. But after some time you are able to
see the other persons sitting in the hall. This happens because
when you were out of the cinema hall where intensity of light
was high, the size of the pupil was small. When you entered the
cinema hall where the intensity of light is low, the size of the
pupil is insufficient to bring in the required amount of light. By
involuntary muscle control the size of pupil increases. Therefore,
after some time you are able to see the other persons sitting in
the hall.

(short-sightedness)
Myopia is a defect in which a human eye can see nearby objects distinctly
but is unable to see distant objects distinctly.
A myopic eye can see near by objects clearly, but is unable

reason that students suffering from myopia are unable to read
writing on black board from back benches.

distant object is first diverged by the concave lens and then
converged by the eye-lens. The power of concave lens is chosen
such that it creates only that much divergence so that after the
converging action of eye-lens the image is formed on the retina.

CATARACT
The eye lens is made up of proteins arranged in a regular pattern. Because
of this regular arrangement the eye-lens is transparent. In some eyes,
the regular pattern gets disturbed and this decreases the transparency
of the eye-lens. If the arrangement disturbs to a greater extent it may
lead to an opaque eye-lens. This is called cataract. This defect is usually
found in old age.
Correction: This defect cannot be corrected by placing a suitable lens
before the eye-lens. Instead, it is corrected by a surgical operation by
replacing the affected lens by an artificial lens.
EYE DONATION
You must have seen advertisment in media persuading for eye
donation. If cornea of the eyes are removed within 6 hours of the death
of a person, it can be transplanted to a person suffering from corneal
blindness. There are more than 45 lakh cases of corneal blindness and
unfortunately out of these a major portion is that of children aged
below 2 years. If a person comes forward for eye donation, he can
save two corneal blind people by donating one eye to each. What one
has to do is go to an eye-bank, fill up the form giving his/her consent
for eye donation. On his/her death, the eye-bank is informed. Persons
from the eye-bank will come home (or in hospital) and remove the
cornea. It takes l0-5 minutes for the removal. The eye taken by the
eye-bank is checked thoroughly for any defect. If found defective it is
Persons who wear spectacles can donate eyes. Even persons having
hypertension, diabetes, etc. can donate eyes. Age is not a bar for eye
donation. But persons who are infected by AIDS, Hepatities B or C,
rabies, acute leukaemia, encephalitis, tetanus cannot donate eyes.
An eye-bank has strict standards to keep the identities of the donor
and recipient confidential. How exciting it feels to think that after one’s
death, she (or he) can make two blind persons see this wonderful world!

The front portion which sharply bulges out is covered with a
transparent and tough membrane called cornea. Behind the cornea
is a region which contains a liquid called aqueous humour. Next to it
is present a circular coloured diaphragm called iris with a hole in its

Behind iris is a crystalline convex lens held in its place by ciliary
muscles. After the lens, the eye is composed of vitreous humour. The
image is formed on a delicate inner-most light-sensitive membrane of the
eye called retina. Retina contains a blind spot where the optic nerve enters
the eye. It is called blind spot because it is totally insensitive to light.

When the intensity of light entering the eye is high, the pupil
contracts so as to reduce the amount of light entering the eye
and vice-versa. The pupil takes some time to adjust its size. You
must have experienced that while entering a cinema hall, it is
difficult to locate your seat. But after some time you are able to
see the other persons sitting in the hall. This happens because
when you were out of the cinema hall where intensity of light
was high, the size of the pupil was small. When you entered the
cinema hall where the intensity of light is low, the size of the
pupil is insufficient to bring in the required amount of light. By
involuntary muscle control the size of pupil increases. Therefore,
after some time you are able to see the other persons sitting in
the hall.

4. DEFECTS OF VISION
Weakening of ciliary muscles, change in the size of eye ball, irregularities
on the surface of cornea, formation of hazy membrane over the eye-lens,
etc. give rise to a number of defects of vision. Let us study these defects.
4.7. Myopia
(short-sightedness)
Myopia is a defect in which a human eye can see nearby objects distinctly
but is unable to see distant objects distinctly.
A myopic eye can see near by objects clearly, but is unable
to see distant object clearly. This is because rays coming from
infinity are converged before retina (see Fig 4 (b). The far point
which should be infinity has come closer and is at a distance
'x’ from eye, see Fig 4(a). This is shown by point 'F'. This point
is generally a few metres from the eye. It is because of this
reason that students suffering from myopia are unable to read
writing on black board from back benches.

(a) High converging power of eye-lens because ciliary
muscles do not relax sufficiently.
(b) Eye ball being longer than normal because of which
the distance between eye-lens and retina increases.

concave lens before the eye. The parallel rays coming from
distant object is first diverged by the concave lens and then
converged by the eye-lens. The power of concave lens is chosen
such that it creates only that much divergence so that after the
converging action of eye-lens the image is formed on the retina.

CATARACT
The eye lens is made up of proteins arranged in a regular pattern. Because
of this regular arrangement the eye-lens is transparent. In some eyes,
the regular pattern gets disturbed and this decreases the transparency
of the eye-lens. If the arrangement disturbs to a greater extent it may
lead to an opaque eye-lens. This is called cataract. This defect is usually
found in old age.
Correction: This defect cannot be corrected by placing a suitable lens
before the eye-lens. Instead, it is corrected by a surgical operation by
replacing the affected lens by an artificial lens.
EYE DONATION
You must have seen advertisment in media persuading for eye
donation. If cornea of the eyes are removed within 6 hours of the death
of a person, it can be transplanted to a person suffering from corneal
blindness. There are more than 45 lakh cases of corneal blindness and
unfortunately out of these a major portion is that of children aged
below 2 years. If a person comes forward for eye donation, he can
save two corneal blind people by donating one eye to each. What one
has to do is go to an eye-bank, fill up the form giving his/her consent
for eye donation. On his/her death, the eye-bank is informed. Persons
from the eye-bank will come home (or in hospital) and remove the
cornea. It takes l0-5 minutes for the removal. The eye taken by the
eye-bank is checked thoroughly for any defect. If found defective it is
Persons who wear spectacles can donate eyes. Even persons having
hypertension, diabetes, etc. can donate eyes. Age is not a bar for eye
donation. But persons who are infected by AIDS, Hepatities B or C,
rabies, acute leukaemia, encephalitis, tetanus cannot donate eyes.
An eye-bank has strict standards to keep the identities of the donor
and recipient confidential. How exciting it feels to think that after one’s
death, she (or he) can make two blind persons see this wonderful world!

transparent and tough membrane called cornea. Behind the cornea

When the intensity of light entering the eye is high, the pupil

was high, the size of the pupil was small. When you entered the
cinema hall where the intensity of light is low, the size of the
pupil is insufficient to bring in the required amount of light. By
involuntary muscle control the size of pupil increases. Therefore,
after some time you are able to see the other persons sitting in
the hall.

4.7. Myopia
(short-sightedness)
Myopia is a defect in which a human eye can see nearby objects distinctly
but is unable to see distant objects distinctly.
A myopic eye can see near by objects clearly, but is unable
to see distant object clearly. This is because rays coming from
infinity are converged before retina (see Fig 4 (b). The far point
which should be infinity has come closer and is at a distance
'x’ from eye, see Fig 4(a). This is shown by point 'F'. This point
is generally a few metres from the eye. It is because of this
reason that students suffering from myopia are unable to read
writing on black board from back benches.

converging action of eye-lens the image is formed on the retina.

CATARACT
The eye lens is made up of proteins arranged in a regular pattern. Because
of this regular arrangement the eye-lens is transparent. In some eyes,
the regular pattern gets disturbed and this decreases the transparency
of the eye-lens. If the arrangement disturbs to a greater extent it may
lead to an opaque eye-lens. This is called cataract. This defect is usually
found in old age.
Correction: This defect cannot be corrected by placing a suitable lens
before the eye-lens. Instead, it is corrected by a surgical operation by
replacing the affected lens by an artificial lens.
EYE DONATION
You must have seen advertisment in media persuading for eye
donation. If cornea of the eyes are removed within 6 hours of the death
of a person, it can be transplanted to a person suffering from corneal
blindness. There are more than 45 lakh cases of corneal blindness and
unfortunately out of these a major portion is that of children aged
below 2 years. If a person comes forward for eye donation, he can
save two corneal blind people by donating one eye to each. What one
has to do is go to an eye-bank, fill up the form giving his/her consent
for eye donation. On his/her death, the eye-bank is informed. Persons
from the eye-bank will come home (or in hospital) and remove the
cornea. It takes l0-5 minutes for the removal. The eye taken by the
eye-bank is checked thoroughly for any defect. If found defective it is
Persons who wear spectacles can donate eyes. Even persons having
hypertension, diabetes, etc. can donate eyes. Age is not a bar for eye
donation. But persons who are infected by AIDS, Hepatities B or C,
rabies, acute leukaemia, encephalitis, tetanus cannot donate eyes.
An eye-bank has strict standards to keep the identities of the donor
and recipient confidential. How exciting it feels to think that after one’s
death, she (or he) can make two blind persons see this wonderful world!

The eye lens is made up of proteins arranged in a regular pattern. Because
of this regular arrangement the eye-lens is transparent. In some eyes,
the regular pattern gets disturbed and this decreases the transparency
of the eye-lens. If the arrangement disturbs to a greater extent it may
lead to an opaque eye-lens. This is called cataract. This defect is usually
found in old age.
Correction: This defect cannot be corrected by placing a suitable lens
before the eye-lens. Instead, it is corrected by a surgical operation by
replacing the affected lens by an artificial lens.

The front portion which sharply bulges out is covered with a
transparent and tough membrane called cornea. Behind the cornea
is a region which contains a liquid called aqueous humour. Next to it
is present a circular coloured diaphragm called iris with a hole in its
centre called pupil.
Behind iris is a crystalline convex lens held in its place by ciliary
muscles. After the lens, the eye is composed of vitreous humour. The
image is formed on a delicate inner-most light-sensitive membrane of the
eye called retina. Retina contains a blind spot where the optic nerve enters
the eye. It is called blind spot because it is totally insensitive to light.

When the intensity of light entering the eye is high, the pupil
contracts so as to reduce the amount of light entering the eye
and vice-versa. The pupil takes some time to adjust its size. You
must have experienced that while entering a cinema hall, it is
difficult to locate your seat. But after some time you are able to
see the other persons sitting in the hall. This happens because
when you were out of the cinema hall where intensity of light
was high, the size of the pupil was small. When you entered the
cinema hall where the intensity of light is low, the size of the
pupil is insufficient to bring in the required amount of light. By
involuntary muscle control the size of pupil increases. Therefore,
after some time you are able to see the other persons sitting in
the hall.

When light passes through air, it is first absorbed by air molecules,
dust particle, smoke, small water droplets and then re-radiated in various
directions. This phenomenon is called scattering. Scattering is also shown
by water droplets present in clouds, dispersed phase particles in a colloidal
solution (Tyndall effect) etc. Due to scattering of light the particles shine
and become visible.

The sun should be seen by the observer when
it reaches the horizon because in this case, the sun
is in the direct line of sight of observer. But sun
is seen before it reaches the horizon. This can be
explained by atmospheric refraction. As a ray of
light from the sun enters the earth’s atmosphere, it
follows a curved path as shown in Fig. 9 due to
atmospheric refraction and reaches the observer. It
appears to the observer as if the rays are coming
from I and, therefore, sun is seen by the observer
at I. Remember that an image is seen along the final
direction of the ray reaching the eye. The sun is seen
two minutes before the sun reaches the horizon.

two minutes after the sun has gone below horizon. Therefore, the duration of
day increases by four minutes due to atmospheric refraction.

coming from a point source is effected by the atmospheric changes. A planet
is nearer as compared to stars. Therefore, a planet appears bigger as well. It

remains the same. Therefore, planets do not twinkle.

front_matter_pages.text:
We feel pleasure in bringing out our multicolour book "Modern’s abc + of
Science (Physics)" for class X students. The book has been prepared according to
the syllabus and the scheme of C.B.S.E.
Salient Features of the Book—
Text matter has been presented in a simple language and interesting style and
in tune with the N.C.E.R.T. textbook.
The text has been supplemented with a large number of neatly well-labelled
diagrams.
The topics are supported by important notes, facts to know, do you know, key
point that strengthen the fundamental concepts to young scholars.
Assignments are provided in each chapter in the light of new pattern, Practice
Exercises and Activities.
Assignments in each chapters provide specially designed questions (solved as
well as unsolved) for covering all types of questions; very short answer type,
short answer type, long answer type and multiple choice questions.
NCERT FILE at the end of each chapter provides solutions to In-Text Questions,
Exercise Questions and Exemplar Problems.
A number of Higher Order Thinking Skills (HOTS) questions with answers are
given at the end of each chapter.
Multiple Choice Questions (MCQs) for competitive examinations are given in
Revision Exercise.
Latest NTSE (SAT) Questions are given in Competition File at the end of each
chapter.
The book provides complete coverage of previous years’ CBSE Board
Examinations.
We hope that the book will be warmly received by the teachers and the
students. Suggestions for further improvements of the book will be gratefully
acknowledged.
Sunil Batra

THEME : MATERIALS
Unit I: Chemical Substances-Nature and Behaviour
(55 Periods)
Chemical reactions: Chemical equation, Balanced chemical equation, implications of a balanced chemical
equation, types of chemical reactions: combination, decomposition, displacement, double displacement,
precipitation, neutralization, oxidation and reduction.
Acids, bases and salts: Their definitions in terms of furnishing of निu and OH ions, General properties,
examples and uses, concept of pH scale (Definition relating to logarithm not required), importance of pH in
everyday life; preparation and uses of Sodium Hydroxide, Bleaching powder, Baking soda, Washing soda
and Plaster of Paris.
Metals and non-metals: Properties of metals and non-metals; Reactivity series; Formation and properties
of ionic compounds; Basic metallurgical processes; Corrosion and its prevention.
Carbon compounds: Covalent bonding in carbon compounds. Versatile nature of carbon. Homologous
series. Nomenclature of carbon compounds containing functional groups (halogens, alcohol, ketones,
aldehydes, alkanes and alkynes), difference between saturated hydrocarbons and unsaturated
hydrocarbons. Chemical properties of carbon compounds (combustion, oxidation, addition and
substitution reaction). Ethanol and Ethanoic acid (only properties and uses), soaps and detergents.
Periodic classification of elements: Need for classification, Early attempts at classification of elements
(Dobereiner’s Triads, Newland’s Law of Octaves, Mendeleev’s Periodic Table), Modern periodic table,
gradation in properties, valency, atomicnumber, metallic and non-metallic properties.
THEME:THE WORLD OF THE LIVING
Unit II : World of Living
(50 Periods)
Life processes: ‘Living Being’. Basic concept of nutrition, respiration, transport and excretion in plants and
animals.
Control and co-ordination in animals and plants: Tropic movements in plants; Introduction of plant
hormones; Control and co-ordination in animals: Nervous system; Voluntary, involuntary and reflex
action; Chemical co-ordination: animal hormones.
Reproduction: Reproduction in animals and plants (asexual and sexual) reproductive health-need and
methods of family planning. Safe sex vs HIV/AIDS. Child bearing and women’s health.
Heredity and Evolution: Heredity; Mendel’s contribution- Laws for inheritance of traits: Sex determination:
brief introduction; Basic concepts of evolution.

front_matter_pages.text:
Unit III : Natural Phenomena
(23 Periods)
Reflection of light by curved surfaces; Images formed by spherical mirrors, centre of curvature, principal
axis, principal focus, focal length, mirror formula (Derivation not required), magnification.
Refraction; Laws of refraction, refractive index.
Refraction of light by spherical lens; Image formed by spherical lenses; Lens formula (Derivation not
required); Magnification. Power of a lens;
Functioning of a lens in human eye, defects of vision and their corrections, applications of spherical mirrors
and lenses.
Refraction of light through a prism, dispersion of light, scattering of light, applications in daily life.
Unit IV : Effects of Current
हिN
(32 Periods)
Electric current, potential difference-and electric current. Ohm’s law; Resistance, Resistivity, Factors on
which the resistance of a conductor depends. Series combination of resistors, parallel combination of
resistors and its applications in daily life. Heating effect of electric current and its applications in daily life.
Electric power, Interrelation between P, V,landR.
Magnetic effects of current: Magnetic field, field lines, field due to a current carrying conductor, field due to
current carrying coil or solenoid; Force on current carrying conductor, Fleming’s Left Hand Rule, Electric
Motor, Electromagnetic induction. Induced potential difference, Induced current. Fleming’s Right Hand
Rule, Electric Generater, Direct current. Alternating current : frequency of AC. Advantage of AC over DC.
Domestic electric circuits.
Unit V : Natural Resources
(20 Periods)
Sources of energy: Different forms of energy, conventional and non-conventional sources of energy: Fossil
fuels, solar energy; biogas; wind, water and tidal energy; Nuclear energy. Renewable versus non-renewable
sources of energy.
Our environment: Eco-system, Environmental problems, Ozone depletion, waste production and their
solutions. Biodegradable and non-biodegradable substances
Management of natural resources: Conservation and judicious use of natural resources. Forest and wild life;
Coal and Petroleum conservation. Examples of people’s participation for conservation of natural resources.
Big dams: Advantages and limitations; alternatives, if any. Water harvesting. Sustainability of natural
resources.

We feel pleasure in bringing out our multicolour book "Modern’s abc + of
Science (Physics)" for class X students. The book has been prepared according to
the syllabus and the scheme of C.B.S.E.
Salient Features of the Book—
Text matter has been presented in a simple language and interesting style and
in tune with the N.C.E.R.T. textbook.
The text has been supplemented with a large number of neatly well-labelled
diagrams.
The topics are supported by important notes, facts to know, do you know, key
point that strengthen the fundamental concepts to young scholars.
Assignments are provided in each chapter in the light of new pattern, Practice
Exercises and Activities.
Assignments in each chapters provide specially designed questions (solved as
well as unsolved) for covering all types of questions; very short answer type,
short answer type, long answer type and multiple choice questions.
NCERT FILE at the end of each chapter provides solutions to In-Text Questions,
Exercise Questions and Exemplar Problems.
A number of Higher Order Thinking Skills (HOTS) questions with answers are
given at the end of each chapter.
Multiple Choice Questions (MCQs) for competitive examinations are given in
Revision Exercise.
Latest NTSE (SAT) Questions are given in Competition File at the end of each
chapter.
The book provides complete coverage of previous years’ CBSE Board
Examinations.
We hope that the book will be warmly received by the teachers and the
students. Suggestions for further improvements of the book will be gratefully
acknowledged.
Sunil Batra

THEME : MATERIALS
Unit I: Chemical Substances-Nature and Behaviour
(55 Periods)
Chemical reactions: Chemical equation, Balanced chemical equation, implications of a balanced chemical
equation, types of chemical reactions: combination, decomposition, displacement, double displacement,
precipitation, neutralization, oxidation and reduction.
Acids, bases and salts: Their definitions in terms of furnishing of निu and OH ions, General properties,
examples and uses, concept of pH scale (Definition relating to logarithm not required), importance of pH in
everyday life; preparation and uses of Sodium Hydroxide, Bleaching powder, Baking soda, Washing soda
and Plaster of Paris.
Metals and non-metals: Properties of metals and non-metals; Reactivity series; Formation and properties
of ionic compounds; Basic metallurgical processes; Corrosion and its prevention.
Carbon compounds: Covalent bonding in carbon compounds. Versatile nature of carbon. Homologous
series. Nomenclature of carbon compounds containing functional groups (halogens, alcohol, ketones,
aldehydes, alkanes and alkynes), difference between saturated hydrocarbons and unsaturated
hydrocarbons. Chemical properties of carbon compounds (combustion, oxidation, addition and
substitution reaction). Ethanol and Ethanoic acid (only properties and uses), soaps and detergents.
Periodic classification of elements: Need for classification, Early attempts at classification of elements
(Dobereiner’s Triads, Newland’s Law of Octaves, Mendeleev’s Periodic Table), Modern periodic table,
gradation in properties, valency, atomicnumber, metallic and non-metallic properties.
THEME:THE WORLD OF THE LIVING
Unit II : World of Living
(50 Periods)
Life processes: ‘Living Being’. Basic concept of nutrition, respiration, transport and excretion in plants and
animals.
Control and co-ordination in animals and plants: Tropic movements in plants; Introduction of plant
hormones; Control and co-ordination in animals: Nervous system; Voluntary, involuntary and reflex
action; Chemical co-ordination: animal hormones.
Reproduction: Reproduction in animals and plants (asexual and sexual) reproductive health-need and
methods of family planning. Safe sex vs HIV/AIDS. Child bearing and women’s health.
Heredity and Evolution: Heredity; Mendel’s contribution- Laws for inheritance of traits: Sex determination:
brief introduction; Basic concepts of evolution.

Electricity
INTRODUCTION
The wonderful discoveries made in science have transformed the
manner in which we live. One such discovery which may be termed
as the most important one is electric current.
Some practical examples of electric current are in household
wiring, in an electric bulb, in picture tube of a television set, in a cell
of a torch, and so on. Nerve current is responsible for transmitting
electric signals in our body.
The form of energy associated with electric current is called
electric energy. This energy can be transmitted very easily from
one place to other with the help of electrical wires. Further it is very
convenient to control and use.
2, ELECTRIC CHARGE
A property associated with objects due to which they show
electrical and magnetic phenomena is called charge. Charges are of
two types— positive and negative. Any object around us is ultimately
made up of atoms. These atoms are made up of protons, neutrons and
electrons. Proton is a positively charged particle present in the nucleus
of an atom. Electrons are negatively charged particles which revolve
around the nucleus. The charge of a proton is equal and opposite to
that of an electron. An atom is electrically neutral because number of
protons is equal to number of electrons.
Charging of an object
Anatom can be charged if the number of protons is made unequal
to the number of electrons. Thus, any object which is charged has
unequal number of protons and electrons.
One method of charging an object is by rubbing it with another
suitable object. For example, if we rub a glass rod with silk cloth, the
glass rod develops a positive charge and silk cloth an equal negative
charge. Where did this charge come from? No new charges have been
created during this process. Electrons move from glass rod to silk cloth.
This makes glass rod positively charged, and silk cloth negatively charged.

page_extractions.text:
I. Insulators: These materials do not conduct electricity. This is because
there are no free charges available for conduction of electricity in these
materials. Examples are rubber, glass, plastics, etc.
2.
Semiconductors: These materials conduct electricity to a certain extent. This
is because a small number of free charges are available for conduction of
electricity. Examples are silicon, germanium, etc.
The modern civilisation is based on semi-conductor devices. The mobile
phones, computers, communication hardware, computer games are semi-
conductor devices.
3.
Conductors: These materials conduct electricity freely. This is because these
materials contain billions and billions of free charges. Examples are all
metals, molten salts, electrolytic solutions etc. These substances are used
in household wiring, in electrical appliances like fans, mixers, washing
machines, etc.
4.
Superconductors: These materials conduct electricity so freely that there
is absolutely no obstruction to the flow of free charges. No obstruction
means no loss of energy. These materials obviously contain billions and
billions of free charges and the movement of charges takes place without
obstruction. Examples are mercury at 4.2 K, certain alloys at 725 K.
As of now, we do not have superconducting materials which can work at
room temperature. But efforts are on by scientists in this regard.
To understand the cause of flow of charges, we need to understand an
important physical quantity called electric potential.
4. ELECTRIC POTENTIAL
Electric potential is a condition that determines the direction of flow of
charge.

I. Insulators: These materials do not conduct electricity. This is because
there are no free charges available for conduction of electricity in these
materials. Examples are rubber, glass, plastics, etc.
2.
Semiconductors: These materials conduct electricity to a certain extent. This
is because a small number of free charges are available for conduction of
electricity. Examples are silicon, germanium, etc.
The modern civilisation is based on semi-conductor devices. The mobile
phones, computers, communication hardware, computer games are semi-
conductor devices.
3.
Conductors: These materials conduct electricity freely. This is because these
materials contain billions and billions of free charges. Examples are all
metals, molten salts, electrolytic solutions etc. These substances are used
in household wiring, in electrical appliances like fans, mixers, washing
machines, etc.
4.
Superconductors: These materials conduct electricity so freely that there
is absolutely no obstruction to the flow of free charges. No obstruction
means no loss of energy. These materials obviously contain billions and
billions of free charges and the movement of charges takes place without
obstruction. Examples are mercury at 4.2 K, certain alloys at 725 K.
As of now, we do not have superconducting materials which can work at
room temperature. But efforts are on by scientists in this regard.

options. Some part of the water will flow from B to C and the remaining
part will flow from B to D. Imagine, through which pipe the rate of flow
will be more and why ? The rate of flow will be larger for broader pipe.

In circuits used in appliances,
a number of resistors are connected in a

series or in parallel, or a combination of these.

When a number of resistors are joined end to end so that same current flows
through each, the resistors are said to be connected in series.
In the case of a string of bulbs, these bulbs are said to be arranged in series
because the same current passes through each bulb.

.7. Applications of Heating Effect of Current
iL.
Heating effect of current is used in electric toaster, electric water heaters,
The heating element is made up of nichrome, manganin or constantan
because of its high resistivity and high melting point. One more property
which makes these alloys useful for such application is that their resistivity
is not much affected by increase in temperature.
Electric fuse: A fuse is a safety device for circuit and electrical appliances.
A fuse wire has low melting point. When high current passes through
the fuse wire, it melts due to the heating effect of current and the circuit
breaks, thereby protecting the appliance from high current damage. A fuse
is connected in live wire.
The heating element of electric current is also used in electric bulbs. When
electric current passes through the tungsten filament, due to heating effect
of current, the element becomes white hot and emits light. In other words,
tungsten filament becomes incandescent. Tungsten is used as it has a high
melting point of 3380°C. The bulb is filled with chemically inert gases like Ne, Ar as tungsten does not react with these gases.
Ne, Ar as tungsten does not react with these gases.

4. INTRODUCTION
In the last chapter, we studied heating
effect of current. In this chapter, we will study
magnetism and magnetic effect of current. In
magnetism, we will deal with the magnetic
effects of a substance when no current is
flowing in the substance. In magnetic effects of
current we will deal with the magnetic effects
created by the current flowing in a wire.
Fig. 7. A bar magnet.
Magnetism was discovered more than 2500 years ago. Earlier
magnetsweremadefromnaturally occurring substancescalledlodestone

The space around a magnet where its influence (attraction or repulsion)
can be experienced is called the magnetic field of that magnet.
Let us take an example to understand this. Suppose, an iron nail is kept at
P very far from a magnet on a smooth horizontal table. The nail will not move
towards the magnet because there is no influence of the magnet at P. But when
the nail is kept at Q near the magnet, the magnet attracts the nail towards itself.
This is because the magnet has its influence at Q. Thus, point P does not lie in
the magnetic field but point Q does.
Where is the influence of a magnet more on its surface? It has been found
that the influence or the strength of the magnet is more at its ends. These ends are
called the poles of the magnet. One end is called north pole and the other end is
called south pole. We can understand this with the help of an activity.

in a given region can be represented with the help of magnetic field lines. To
draw magnetic field lines we need a plotting magnetic compass. A plotting
magnet consists of a small magnetic needle pivoted in the compass. The needle
is free to move in a horizontal plane. The arrowhead is the north pole and tail
is the south pole.

3. Properties of Magnetic Field Lines
l. Magnetic field lines are imaginary line used to show magnetic field ina
given region.
2. Magnetic field lines are closed continuous curves and are directed from
north pole to south pole outside the magnet and from south pole to north
pole inside the magnet (see Fig. 8).
3. The tangent at any point on the magnetic field line gives the direction of
magnetic field at that point (tangent is a line which just touches a curve
at a point.) This is also the direction of orientation of the needle of the
magnetic compass if kept at that point (see Fig. 9).
4. Magnetic field lines are closer together (crowded) in the region where
the magnetic field is strong (at P) and are widely separated in the region
where the magnetic field is weak (at Q) (see Fig. 0).
5. Magnetic field lines do not intersect each other. This is because
if you place the magnetic compass at the point of intersection it
will orient itself only in one direction and not in two directions
(see Fig. ).

The magnetic field of an electromagnet depends on:

When the electric current is switched off, the electromagnet loses its
magnetism instantaneously. From this, it can be clearly interpreted that the
soft iron also loses its magnetism as soon as the current is switched off. The
second important conclusion is that an electromagnet is a temporary magnet. It
behaves as a magnet only when current is flowing through it.
Uses of Electromagnets
(a) For electrical devices such as electric trains.
(b) For moving big objects of iron from one place to another.
(c) For removing small iron splinter from an eye of a patient.
7. PERMANENT MAGNET
If we keep hard steel in place of soft iron in a solenoid and switch on
the current for some time, then hard steel converts into a magnet. But when
the current is switched off, the hard steel does not lose its magnetism. This
means that hard steel converts into a permanent magnet. Therefore, to make
a permanent magnet, a magnetic material is kept in the strong magnetic field
(like that present inside a solenoid).
Magnetic Materials
Not every material can be converted into a magnet. Certain materials which
are used to make permanent magnets are carbon steel, chromium steel, cobalt
and tungsten steel. Some alloys are alnico (an alloy of aluminium, nickel,
cobalt and iron) and Nipermag (an alloy of aluminium, nickel, and iron).
Uses: Permanent magnets find use in microphones, loudspeakers,
ammeters, voltmeters, speedometers, electric clocks, etc.

If we keep hard steel in place of soft iron in a solenoid and switch on

ammeters, voltmeters, speedometers, electric clocks, etc.

2. ELECTROMAGNETIC INDUCTION
One of the most important discovery of Michael Faraday is producing
induced current with the help of magnetic force. In other words, we can say
that Faraday produced electricity from magnetism, a phenomenon called
electromagnetic induction. How can electric current be produced by magnetic
force? Let us understand this phenomenon by the following activities.
2.. Activity
(a) The adjacent diagram Fig. 26 (a) shows a bar magnet at rest with
respect to the metallic coil C. The coil is connected to a sensitive
galvanometer. The reading in the galvanometer is zero.
(b) When the north pole of a magnet is being moved towards the coil,
the galvanometer shows some deflection in Fig. 26 (b). This means
that a current is flowing in the coil (without the help of a battery).
This current is called induced current. The current remains in the
circuit till the magnet is moving with respect to coil. When there is no
relative motion, the reading in the galvanometer is zero. Current is
produced because a potential difference is developed across the coil.
This potential difference is also called induced emf (electromotive
force).
2... Reason for induced current
It has been observed that whenever there is a change in the number of magnetic
field lines* passing through a coil, an induced emf
is produced and an induced current
flows in the coil. In the above case, the number of magnetic lines of force through the
coil increases.
(c) When the bar magnet is moved away from the coil, again the needle
of the galvanometer shows deflection but in the opposite direction
[see Fig. 26 (c)].
Again, the number of magnetic lines of force through the coil changes. In
the above case, the number of magnetic line of force decreases.
It is important to note that it is not necessary to move the magnet and keep
the coil stationary. In fact, you can create the same effect by
(a) bringing the coil near the magnet and keeping the magnet stationary.
(e) taking the coil away from the magnet, keeping the magnet stationary.
(f) bringing the south pole near the coil or taking the south pole away
from the coil. The above activities will bring a change in the number
of magnetic lines of forces passing through the coil and thus can
produce induced emf and induced current.
2.2 Activity 2
Fig. 27. shows two coils (1, 2) of copper wire of large number of turns mounted on a thick paper roll. Coil 1 is connected to a battery B with a key K.
mounted on a thick paper roll. Coil I is connected to a battery B with a key K.
Coil 2 is connected to a sensitive Galvanometer G.
When the key K is closed, a current starts building up in coil 7. As the
current increases in magnitude, the magnetic field created by this current
also increases which increases the number of magnetic lines of force. These
magnetic lines of force also cross from coil 2. Therefore, magnetic lines of force
passing through coil 2 increases, creating an induced current in coil 2 which
can be observed by noticing the deflection in the galvanometer.

Concept
3. FARADAY’S LAWS OF ELECTROMAGNETIC INDUCTION
Electromagnetic induction is the phenomenon in which an induced emf
and induced current is produced in a coil by changing magnetic field (change
in the number of magnetic field lines) through it.
The above facts can be summarised in the following laws proposed by
Faraday.
(9. Achange in the number of magnetic field lines (magnetic flux) through a
loop produces an induced emf and induced current in the loop.
(2) The magnitude of induced emf and induced current depends on the change
in the number of magnetic field lines through the loop with respect to
time.
4. DIRECTION OF INDUCED CURRENT: FLEMING’S RIGHT
HAND RULE
Stretch the thumb, the forefinger and the central finger of your right hand
so that these are perpendicular to each other. First, orient your hand such that
the forefinger points towards the magnetic field, then rotate your hand such
that the forefinger remains pointing towards the magnetic field but the thumb
points in the direction of motion of the conductor, then the central finger gives
the direction of the induced current. Refer Fig. 28
Caution: Do not use Fleming’s left hand rule in finding the direction of
induced current. It has been observed that a common mistake a student makes
is to use Fleming’s left-hand rule when Fleming’s right-hand rule has to be
applied.

Note: The direction of induced current is such that it opposes the change
in the number of magnetic field lines. If north pole of bar magnet is brought
towards a loop, current will flow in the loop and create its own magnetic field.
The magnetic field of current produces north pole towards that side where the
north pole of bar magnet is approaching. In this way, it can resist the approach
If north pole of bar magnet is approaching, in this way, it can induce current in the coil. If south pole of bar magnet approaches a coil, it can also induce current [see Fig. 29].
If south pole of bar magnet approaches a coil, induced current will flow in
the coil such that south pole of the magnetic field due to current is created on
that side where south pole of bar magnet is approaching.
Similarly, if north pole of bar magnet is going away from the coil, the
current flows such that south pole is created on the side where north pole of
bar magnet is receding (to oppose change in magnetic field lines).
5. DIRECT CURRENT
Tf current flows always in the same direction, the current is called direct
current.
The source of direct current is generally a cell or a battery or a d.c.
generator.
Graphically, the current is represented as shown in the Fig. 3. This current
is direct because it always has a positive value and is steady because its value

What keeps live wire at 220 V? If you observe, you will find that the main
electric meter of your house is connected to the electric pole outside your
house with two wires. Out of these two wire one is live wire (L) and the other
is neutral wire (N). Since the live wire at electric pole is at 220 V, the live wire
of your house is also at 220 V. Now, the question arises that what keeps the
live wire on the electric pole wire at 220 V. The electric pole wire is connected

5. House Wiring: The different electrical appliances used in a house
(like fan, tubelight, T.V, bulb, washing machine) are connected in
parallel with a switch in the live wire for every parallel branch.
The reason for connecting the appliances in parallel is that if one
appliance becomes faulty, then it does not affect the working of
other appliances. Suppose, the appliances are connected in series,
then if an appliance becomes faulty and no current passes through
it, then no current will pass to the other appliances as well. Due to
one faulty appliance, not even a single appliance can be run. Parallel
arrangement of appliances also ensures a voltage of 220 V across all
appliances.
Moreover, if electrical appliances are connected in series, either all
appliances will have to run together or switched off together. What a funny
situation it would be?
The electrical wiring in our house can be divided into two parts.
(a) Circuit with appliances which uses a maximum of 5 ampere of
current. These appliances are bulbs, tubelights, fans, radio, T.V.,
etc. The copper wire used in the circuit is thin. This circuit is
connected with a 5 A fuse.
(b) Circuit with appliances which uses a current greater than
Circuit with appliances which uses a current greater than 5 ampere but less than 15 ampere. The copper wire used in this circuit is thick. This circuit is connected with a 15 A fuse.
circuit is thick. This circuit is connected with a 5 A fuse.
20. ELECTRIC FUSE
Electric fuse is a safety device which protects the circuit and electrical
appliances from damage due to high current.
An electric fuse works on the principle of heating effect current. It is made
up of a wire of an alloy of tin and lead (63% tin and 37% lead). It has low
melting point.
When rated current flows in the wire, the fuse wire remains connected
and current flows. But if current more than the rated current flows, the heat
produced (I°Rt) in the fuse wire is enough to melt it (due to low melting point
of fuse wire). The current does not flow through the fuse wire (circuit breaks)
and, therefore, does not reach the appliance thus saving it from burning off
(see Fig. 47).

The direction of induced current can be found by Fleming’s right-hand rule.
Induced emf and induced current are also produced in a conductor when magnetic lines of force perpendicular
to its length are cut by the movement of the conductor.
If current flows always in the same direction, the current is called direct current.
If current changes its direction after regular intervals of time, the current is said to be alternating current.
A generator is a device which converts mechanical energy into electrical energy.
An a.c. generator is based on the principle of electromagnetic induction. In an a.c. generator, the armature is
connected with slip-rings.
A d.c. generator is based on the principle of electromagnetic induction. In a d.c. generator the armature is
connected with split-rings.
In domestic electric circuits,
(a) The red-coloured insulation on copper wire is live wire, the black coloured insulation on copper wire
is neutral wire, the green-coloured insulation on wire is earthing wire.
(b) All appliances are connected in parallel.
The advantages of a.c. over d.c. is that
(a) the voltage can be changed easily.
(b) power distribution losses can be reduced.
Electric fuse is a safety device which protects the circuit and electrical appliances from damage.
An electric fuse is made up of an alloy of tin and lead (63% tin and 37% lead).
If a number of large current-drawing appliances are switched on at the same time, high current is drawn. This
condition is called overloading.
When live wire comes in contact with the neutral wire directly, high current passes through the circuit. This
condition is called short circuiting.

The function of earth wire in an electrical
instrument is to save us from electric shocks.
If live wire of electrical instrument is in contact
with the metallic part of the appliance (due to
a fault), then maximum current flows through
the earth wire which is in connection to the
metallic part. Thus if we happen to touch the
lectrical appliance, then negligible current will
flow through us saving us from electric shocks.
When live wire comes in direct contact with
neutral wire, then the electrical appliance gets
by-passed and a large current flows in the
circuit. This is called short cricuiting.

A DISCUSSION
We know that energy is conserved. That is, energy can neither be created nor
destroyed. Then, why do we talk about energy crisis! In fact, when we talk
about energy crisis we mean that energy which we can use to run machines/
vehicles. The two major forms of energy are electricity and fossil fuels. The
energy produced from all sources, falls far short of demand across major parts
of the globe.
Alternative sources of energy are required to meet our present and future
requirements. Such sources are wind energy, water energy, solar energy, tidal
energy, geothermal energy, bioenergy, nuclear energy, etc. Our focus in this chapter
will be on the various sources of energy available to us, the potential of these
sources, how energy can be harnessed through these sources and so on.
2. SOURCE OF ENERGY AND ITS CHARACTERISTICS
A source of energy is one which has the capacity to provide useful energy.
We have to spend some energy to get a source of energy. If the energy spent is
called input energy and the source of energy provides output energy then,
useful energy = output energy - input energy.
Coal is an important source of energy. To use it at a desired place, first we

4. Energy of ocean waves

The first six sources of energy are expected to be available for another
five billion years. This is because these sources of energy are dependent
on the energy from the sun. The sun is expected to last for another five
billion years. So we will continue to draw energy from these six sources till
then.
Nature has gifted us with all these sources which are available free of cost.
These sources of energy are pollution-free except energy from burning wood.
It is not advisable to depend on trees for fulfilling our energy requirements.
Already, trees are being cut down on a massive scale for industrial and
residential purpose to cater the needs of the growing population. Cutting of
trees leads to environmental problems. Instead, we should grow more and
more trees. It should be noted that it takes around 15 years for a tree to grow and mature.
and mature.
5. Energy from biological wastes
Note: If we cut down trees to meet our requirements, then we should first
ensure that sufficient number of trees are planted to maintain the
environmental balance.
Why is nuclear energy considered renewable?
Nuclear energy is often considered to be a renewable source of energy.
However, strictly speaking it is not renewable. The reason for this can be
understood as follows:
Though the reserves of nuclear fuel are limited, these are still taken as
renewable because the usage of this fuel is in minute quantities and therefore,
this source of energy will last for a very long period.
Another way of classification of sources of energy
(a) Conventional sources of energy
The sources of energy which have been in use for a long time and are a major
source of energy are called conventional sources of energy.
Examples are-fossil fuels, energy of flowing water, wind energy, biomass
energy (use of dung cakes).
(b) Non-conventional sources energy
The sources of energy which are relatively new and are not a major source of
energy are called non-conventional sources of energy.
Examples are—tidal energy, wave energy, ocean thermal energy, geothermal
energy, nuclear energy and solar energy.
Advantages of Classification of Energy
l. It brigs into focus the energy crisis and a thinking to use non-renewable
sources judiciously.
2. It also brings into focus the need to look and use alternative or non-
conventional sources of energy.

relatively short period of time are called non-renewable sources of energy.

3. Coal

Precautions in using LPG: LPG leakage can lead to fire and burns.
Therefore, the following precautions should be strictly observed:
l. The rubber tubing should be checked at regular intervals for cracks
or holes. If observed, it should be replaced immediately by a rubber
tubing of recommended standards.
Even if no cracks are found, the rubber tubing should still be replaced
after its recommended life-span is over.
2. The gas burners should be of recommended standards.
3. The valve of the regulator of the gas cylinder should be kept closed
when not in use.

small amounts. Mercaptan gas is a foul smelling gas. This is done to
detect leakage of LPG as soon as possible. If leakage is detected,
(a) no electrical switch should be turned off or on. This is because a
small spark is produced on turning an electrical switch off or on
which may ignite LPG. Because of the same reason, do not light
a matchstick.
(b) all doors and windows should be opened so that the gas may
escape.

Natural gas is formed by anaerobic fermentation of organic matter buried
under seabeds millions of years ago.

nitrogen, oxygen, and hydrogen sulphide.
It is found deep in earth’s crust either alone or along with crude oil
deposits. It is obtained by drilling wells.
The largest reservoirs of natural gas is found in former Soviet Union
and Middle East. In India, it is found in offshore areas of Mumbai, Krishna-
Godavari delta, Jaisalmer, etc. The total deposits of natural gas in India are
estimated at over 00 billion cubic metres.

4. Itis used to prepare hydrogen which is further used for the manufacture

It is a clean fuel (it does not leave residue)
In the form of CNG, it is transported through pipelines.
It has high calorific value (55 kJ / g)
It is an attractive substitute for diesel and petrol.

4.5 Disadvantages of using Fossil Fuels
Elements like carbon, nitrogen and sulphur are present in fossil fuels.
When fossil fuels are burnt, these elements react with oxygen of air to
produce oxides which are acidic in nature. This leads to acid rain which
adversely affects the quality of water and soil.
2. CO, is a gas which produces greenhouse effect. This leads to global
warming.
3. CO produced is a toxic gas.
How can pollution created by fossil fuels be decreased?
l. By ensuring complete combustion so that CO is not produced.
2. By trapping harmful substances to be released in air along with the
exhaust of combustion. Catalytic converters are used in vehicles for
this purpose. Similarly, electrostatic precipitators are used in industrial
boilers.

7. ENERGY FROM FLOWING WATER (HYDRO ENERGY)
Flowing water possesses kinetic energy. Flowing water is available in
rivers which is a big and important source of energy.
7. What Causes Water to Flow?
When sun rays fall on water bodies, water evaporates and water vapour is
formed. This water vapour rises in the atmosphere from a height of
km to
5 km forming clouds. Wind blows these clouds from one region to another.
Ultimately, the water vapour converts into rain and snow and falls back on
earth. The snow on the mountains melt and water from rainfall flows down
in rivers.
Thus, we may conclude that energy possessed by flowing water is an
indirect source of solar energy.
Flowing water, as a source of energy, has been used for centuries to
transport heavy logs of wood from one place to another, to grind cereals by
water mills, to channelise water through canals for irrigation, etc. A better way
to harness the energy of flowing water is by converting it into electrical energy.
Let us study how this can be done.

A power station where the kinetic energy of flowing water in river is
converted into electrical energy is called hydroelectric power plant and
_ the electricity produced is called hydroelectricity.
Hydroelectric power plant.

The water stored in a dam is allowed to fall down thereby converting the
potential energy of stored water into kinetic energy. This flowing water rotates

water is allowed to flow down where a turbine (T) is situated. This turbine is
connected to the armature of a generator (G).

potential energy of the stored water is converted into kinetic energy of flowing
water. When this flowing water, which possesses high kinetic energy strikes

Traditional Chulhas
Wood, agricultural waste and animal dung cakes are a major source of
energy (around 80%) in rural areas. These are burnt in traditional chulhas to
cook food. The traditional chulha has the following disadvantages:
(a) The efficiency is very low (around 8%) as most of the heat produced by
burning the fuel is lost to the surroundings.
(b) It produces a lot of smoke due to incomplete combustion which is not
good for health.
(c) Ash is produced as residue.
Smokeless Chulhas
To eliminate the disadvantages of traditional chulhas, smokeless chulhas
were designed. The smokeless chulhas have a chimney for removal of exhaust
gas. The design of smokeless chulhas ensures proper supply of air. It allows
almost complete combustion of fuel. This helps in two ways:
(a) High efficiency: Much more heat is obtained by burning same amount of
fuel in smokeless chulhas as compared to traditional chulhas.
Moreover, loss of heat to the surroundings is less in smokeless chulhas.
(b) Smoke free atmosphere.
0. CHARCOAL
Charcoal is a fuel obtained by heating wood strongly in the absence of air.
The process of heating a material containing carbon compounds (wood or
coal) in the absence of air is called destructive distillation. Therefore, we can
say that charcoal is obtained by destructive distillation of wood.
0.7. Charcoal is a Better Fuel than Wood
Wood is a mixture of carbon compounds containing carbon, hydrogen and
oxygen. When wood is heated, all these atoms do not combine with oxygen to
produce heat. But charcoal is mainly made of carbon atoms. When charcoal is
burnt, all the carbon atoms combine with oxygen to produce heat. Therefore,
charcoal has the following advantages over wood as a fuel:
(a) Charcoal has higher calorific value than wood. This means that we
get more heat energy by burning one gram of charcoal as compared to
wood. The calorific value of charcoal is approximately twice that of the
wood.
(b) Charcoal does not produce smoke on burning.
(c) Charcoal is a light and compact fuel and is easy to handle.
(d) Charcoal burns without flames.
But one has to pay more for charcoal as compared to wood. This is because
about | kg of wood on destructive distillation produces only 0.25 kg of charcoal.
ANIMAL DUNG AS A FUEL
In villages, dung cakes made from animal dung are used as fuel in
chulhas. This is not a good method of using animal dung due to the following
limitations:
(a) Low calorific value is obtained.

14.6 Wind Energy Farm The electricity produced
The electricity produced by a single windmill has no practical importance.
Therefore,
a number of windmills are installed over a large area of land called wind
energy farm.
The output of each wind mill is coupled together to generate electricity
which can be used for commercial purpose.
Note: The wind velocity is not the same at all places and at all heights. The
design of the shape and number of blades, the height of windmill
depends on the average wind velocity at that place.

5.6 Solar Cell
A device which converts solar radiations directly into electricity is called
a solar cell.
A solar cell is a better device to produce electricity as compared to solar power
towers because it does not involve water, steam turbines, dynamo, etc. It took
around 00 years for the technology of solar cells to develop to the level we
see today!
The first solar cell was made of a wafer (thin sheet) of selenium which
had an efficiency of only 0.7% and thus was not practical for generating
electricity. In 954, the first practical solar cell was made which could
convert % of solar energy falling on it into electricity. This efficiency was
also low. Solar cells were in demand for space research programmes and for using
electricity at remote places. Therefore, efforts were on to design a solar cell of
higher efficiency.

5.7 Solar Cell Panel
To run various devices like water pump, radio, street lighting in remote
areas and in artificial satellite, electricity is required. The remote areas and
artificial satellite cannot be connected to overhead electrical wires coming from
power generation plants. It is here that the electricity requirement can be fulfilled
by solar cells. But a single solar cell produces electricity at the rate of 0.7 J/s or
0.7 W which is small. Therefore, a number of solar cells are joined together in
a particular pattern so that electrical power generated is enough for practical
usage. Thus, we can say that:
A solar cell panel consists of a large number of solar cells joined together
in a particular pattern.
Advantages of Solar Cell Panel
Ithas long life.
2.
Itis pollution-free.
3. Requires less maintenance as it has no moving parts.
4.
It is a good choice for remote areas and for artificial satellites, space
probes, etc.
5. Itneeds no focussing device which has to be adjusted time to time.

l. Initial cost is high because the silicon used is of a special grade which
has a high level of purity and is expensive.
2. The wire used for connecting solar cells is of silver, which is expensive.
Silver is used to reduce resistance loss as silver is the best conductor of
electricity.

Conclusion: Tidal energy is not a major source of energy.
6.2 Sea Wave Energy
Another source of energy available in sea is sea wave energy. Wind blows
over the surface of sea producing fast moving sea waves. In other words, the
kinetic energy possessed by fast moving sea waves is because of the wind
blowing over the surface of sea. Wind energy is an indirect source of solar
energy, therefore, energy associated with sea waves is also an indirect source
of solar energy. The kinetic energy associated with sea waves can be utilised
to generate electricity. A number of systems have been designed to convert the
kinetic energy of sea waves into electrical energy. The study of these designs
are beyond the scope of this book.
Potential of Sea Wave Energy
The power associated with sea waves world-wide is estimated to be about
2 × 10^6 - 3 × 10^6 MW. It has also been calculated that to generate commercially
viable electricity by sea wave, the site where the device is proposed to be
established should have an energy density of 40 MW / km.
India has a long coastal belt of about 6000 km which can generate a power
of 40,000 MW.

17. GEOTHERMAL ENERGY
The energy possessed by hot water and steam entrapped between the hot
rocks present below the surface of earth is called geothermal energy.
Itis the underground water which gets converted into hot water and steam,
when it comes in contact with the hot rocks. There are only certain places,
called hot spots, where hot rocks are present. The reason for the rocks to be
hot is that the hot magma present below the crust is pushed upwards between
the rocks due to geological changes. This magma is extremely hot. The high
temperature of magma is because of radioactive substances present in the core
of earth. Therefore, geothermal energy is an indirect form of nuclear energy.
Here, it can be concluded that geothermal energy is not an indirect source of solar
energy.
Turbine
How is this hot water or steam used to generate electricity?
A deep hole is drilled in the earth’s crust which reaches the hot
spot and a pipe is fitted in the hole. The steam coming out of the
hole at high pressure is used to turn the turbine and generate
electricity.
Natural geysers are found at certain places. These are places
where hot water and steam come out of the surface of earth on
their own. This happens in those hot spots where hot water
and steam find their way through cracks in the rocks and come
out. Natural geysers are also used to run turbines and generate
electricity.
Merits of Geothermal Energy
l. Electricity produced is cheap.
2. Itis pollution-free.
3. Electricity can be generated round the clock.

Controlled Nuclear Reaction
A chain nuclear reaction can be controlled to release energy at a rate
which can be handled comfortably to produce electricity. Enrico Fermi, in
942, made a first successful attempt to control fission. A fission of U-235
nucleus emits 2 or 3 fast moving neutrons. Under certain conditions, the
fission reaction can be made self-propagating as well as releasing desired
amount of energy. The following points have to be remembered.
(a) The neutron emitted during fission is of a very high energy
(2 MeV). This energy has to be reduced to (0.0245 eV) to
enable it to trigger another fission reaction. The energy of neutrons
can be decreased by making them collide with special substance
like graphite (C) or heavy water (D,O) called moderators.
(b) The fuel used should be enriched uranium. Naturally occurring
uranium has a low percentage (0.715%) of fissile nucleus U - 235
uranium has a low percentage (0.715%) of fissile nucleus U - 235 and a majority of U - 238. The probability of neutron striking U - 235 nucleus at this low percentage is less. The neutron may be
U - 235 nucleus at this low percentage is less. The neutron may be absorbed by U - 238 nucleus or may escape out. This may stop the
The neutron may be absorbed by U - 238 nucleus or may escape out. This may stop the chain reaction. To avoid this natural occurring uranium is enriched.
chain reaction. To avoid this natural occurring uranium is enriched
to 2 - 5% U - 235 and then used as a fuel.
Also, since neutrons have a good penetrating power, the fuel U - 235 should have a minimum mass which can support a chain reaction.
should have a minimum mass which can support a chain reaction. This
mass is called critical mass and the uranium block of minimum size for
a sustained chain reaction is called critical size. If mass of a block is less
than this, the emitted neutron can move out of the block without trigerring
another fission.
20.3 Nuclear Reactor (Nuclear Power Plant)
A device in which electricity is produced by the process of controlled
nuclear fission reaction is called nuclear reactor.
20.4 Nuclear Energy in India
Developed countries depend heavily on nuclear reactors for their electricity
generation requirements. Around 30% of the total electric power generation is
from nuclear reactors.
In India, only around 3% of the total electric power is generated
through nuclear reactors. The nuclear reactors in operation are: (a) Tarapur
in Maharashtra, (b) Kota in Rajasthan, (c) Kalpakkam in Tamil Nadu and
(4) Narora in Uttar Pradesh. Some other nuclear power plants are in the
pipeline which are expected to become operational soon.
India has major research centres for atomic energy: One of these is Bhabha
Atomic Research Centre (BARC) at Mumbai. Some others are located at
Gulmarg in Srinagar and Kolkata in West Bengal.

Nuclear fusion is a process in which two or more lighter nuclei combine to
form a heavy and stable nucleus resulting in the release of energy.
The mass of products of a nuclear fusion reaction is less than the mass of
the reactants. This difference in mass is converted into energy which can be
calculated by the formula E = mc^2
where, m = mass of reactants - mass of products.

THE GREENHOUSE EFFECT
The solar radiations coming from sun pass through the earth’s atmosphere and
reach the earth’s surface. Most of this energy is absorbed by the earth’s surface.
Some radiations are reflected back by the earth’s surface to space.
Reflected radiations have longer wavelengths. These radiations are trapped by
greenhouse gases (CO,, H,O vapours, CH,, Nitrous oxide) thereby warming the
planet. This is called greenhouse effect.
Higher level of CO, and methane are accumulating in the atmosphere,
enhancing the greenhouse effect and producing global warming. Due to global
warming the temperature of earth is rising because of which polar ice caps has
started melting. This has raised the water level in oceans. The calculations of
scientists show that if the level of greenhouse gases remain rising at the present
level, in a:span of 30-40 years the level of water in oceans will rise to a level
which will submerge a big part of plains. The worst part is that we have no
means to control such global phenomenon, once the gas enter the atmosphere.
Therefore, use of fossil fuels should be reduced to a minimum level.

A source of energy is one which delivers energy at the required rate and required time continuously.
Electrical energy and chemical energy of fossil fuel are the best sources of energy.
A source of energy which can be renewed again and again in a relatively short period of time is called
a renewable source of energy. For example, wind energy, solar energy, energy of flowing water, energy
of ocean waves, energy from biological wastes, energy from burning wood, nuclear energy, geothermal
energy, tidal energy.
The source of energy which cannot be renewed again and again in a relatively short period of time are
called non-renewable source of energy, e.g. fossil fuels.
The plants and animals on earth hundreds of millions of years ago, died and were buried deep inside. Over
time, they were gradually converted by natural process into fossil fuels.
Coal is a mixture of compounds of carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and free carbon. The most inferior quality of
coal is peat which is used as a domestic fuel. Other qualities of coal are lignite, bituminous and anthracite.
Refining of crude petroleum is the process of separating various components of petroleum from one another
by the process of fractional distillation.
LPG (Liquefied Petroleum Gas) is petroleum gas in liquid state. The major constituent of LPG is butane.
Natural gas is a mixture of gaseous hydrocarbon consisting mainly of methane (85%).
CNG (Compressed Natural Gas) is natural gas in liquid state.
A power station where the kinetic energy of flowing water in river is converted into electrical energy is
called hydroelectric power plant and the electricity produced is called hydroelectricity.
Living things, their waste products and dead parts is called biomass. The energy obtained from biomass is
called bio-energy.
Charcoal is a fuel obtained by heating wood strongly in the absence of air (destructive distillation).
Anaerobic micro-organism in the presence of water, decompose the complex carbon compounds present
in biomass into a mixture of gases. This process is called anaerobic degradation.
Biogas is a mixture of gases obtained by anaerobic degradation of biomass in the presence of water.
e The main constituent of biomass is methane.
Fixed dome type biogas plants are better than floating gas holder type biogas plants.
e Manure is a by-product of biogas plants.
The energy possessed by wind due to motion of air molecules is called wind energy.
Awindmill is a device which converts kinetic energy into mechanical or electrical energy.
A number of windmills installed over a large area of land to generate electricity is known as wind energy
farm. For a windmill to operate commercially, the minimum velocity of air required is
15 kmh^ - 1.

m? 0

SOURCES OF
ENERGY
A device which is capable of using solar energy directly as heat or converting it into electricity is called a
solar energy device.
A device used to cook food by utilising the infra-red radiation coming from the sun is called solar cooker.
A device which converts solar radiations directly into electricity is called a solar cell.
The energy associated with rise and fall of water in sea tides is called tidal energy.
Wind blows over the surface of sea, producing fast moving sea waves. The energy associated with sea
waves is called sea wave energy.
The solar energy stored in the form of heat in warm surface water of oceans is called Ocean Thermal Energy
(OTE).
The energy possessed by hot water and steam trapped between the hot rocks present below the surface of
earth is called geothermal energy.
When a nucleus interacts with another nucleus or a particle like neutron resulting in the formation of new
nuclei, the process is called a nuclear reaction.
e
The total charge before and after the nuclear reaction remains the same.
e
The total number of nucleons before and after the nuclear reaction remains the same.
e
The total mass of the products is not equal to reactants. The difference in the mass is converted into
energy. [E = mc^2]
Fissile nuclei are U235 and Pu239,
(a) When an unstable nucleus is bombarded with a suitable projectile it splits up into two medium sized
nuclei, release some neutrons and an enormous amount of energy. This process is called nuclear fission.
(b) When occurrence of one nuclear reaction triggers the occurrence of next nuclear reaction and this
nuclear reaction continues in a self-sustained manner, the reaction is called nuclear chain reaction.
(c) For anuclear chain reaction the fuel should have a minimum mass called critical mass and a minimum
size called critical size. The fuel (U-235) used should be enriched to 2-5%.
(d) Controlled nuclear reaction is used to produce electricity in nuclear reactors.
(e) Uncontrolled nuclear reaction is put to destructive use in atom bombs.
A device in which electricity is produced by the process of controlled nuclear fission reaction is called
nuclear reactor.

present in the core of earth. Geothermal energy is called a
renewable energy source because the water is replenished
by rainfall, and the heat is continuously produced by the
earth. Geothermal reservoirs of steam or hot water occur
naturally where magma comes close enough to the surface
to heat ground water trapped in fractured or porous rocks,
or where water circulates at great depth along faults.
Hot water geothermal reservoirs are the most common
type. To generate electricity, the hot water is piped from
geothermal wells, at low pressure it converts into steam.

electricity. Electricity is now produced from geothermal
energy in 2] countries, including the United States.

water is allowed to pass through a turbine to
generate hydroelectricity.
(ii) Wind blowing over the surface of sea produces
fast moving sea waves. The kinetic energy
associated with sea waves can be utilised to
generate electricity.
3. Solar energy creates unequal heating of land and
water bodies on earth. This creates a pressure
difference in the air above it and wind blows.
4, The reasons are :
(a) Electricity generated from flowing water is
cheaper, as compared to burning coal.
(b) Flowing water is a renewable source of energy
whereas coal is a non-renewable source.
5. A device which converts solar radiation directly into
electricity is called a solar cell. Silicon and germanium are
mostly used for making solar cells.
6. The four characteristics used for selecting a suitable
fuel are
(a) It should deliver energy at the required rate for
the required time continuously.
(b) It should be available at appropriate cost.
(c) It should not produce soot and ash.
(a) It should have appropriate ignition temperature.
7. For box-type solar cooker, plane mirror is the best choice
because it reflects the IR radiation into the box and helps
to create a temperature of 00-40°C in 2 to 3 hours.
8. Coal and crude oil are exhaustible sources of energy.
This is because nature cannot renew these sources of
energy in a relatively short period of time.
9. The requirement of energy is rising tremendously. A
major part of the requirement is being met by fossil
fuels. Fossil fuels, particularly crude oil and natural
gas, will last only for another five to six decades.
What will happen after that? Therefore a lot of efforts
are being made to find alternate sources of energy.

short wavelength infra-red radiations coming from
sun to pass through it. But it reflects large wavelength
infra-red radiations.

are formed which rise up and form clouds. These
clouds produce rainfall and snow fall due to which we
get flowing water. Thus, water flowing in river is an
indirect form of solar energy.

water pumps (to lift ground water).
In India, windmills are located in Gujarat, Rajasthan,

Blue sky, green forests and
rainbows are enjoyed by everyone.
At night, we see twinkling of stars,
beautiful signboards in the market
place. Why does sky look blue at
day-time and black at night? Why

still water
surface ? We will find the answers

2. HOW DO WE SEE OBJECTS
Suppose, you are standing in a darkroom. Will you be able to see
the ceiling fan or the almirah kept in the room? The answer is NO.
Now, if you light a candle in the room, you will not only be able to see
the candle flame but also other objects present in the room. You are
able to see the candle flame because light from the flame reaches your
eyes and falls on the retina. Here, this light is converted into electrical
signals which move to the rear of your brain where you interpret
the information transmitted by light. The system of your brain can
interpret
the
colour,
the
shape, etc., of the objects.
We say that an image is
formed on the retina which
is interpreted by the brain.
A
candle
flame
is
producing its own light and
is called a luminous object.
Such objects which produce
their own light are called
luminous objects.

8. OBJECT AND IMAGE
An object is one which we are looking at or which we want to see. An object
either emits its own light (like sun, bulb, candle flame) or reflects light incident
on it (like chair, table, ball, moon). An object can be seen by the light coming
from it. If the size of object is very small it is called a point object.
Recall the discussion of our visual system given in Article .2. We were
able to see candle flame or a ceiling fan when light rays from these objects
were falling on our eyes. This means that light rays from, say, the ceiling fan
were converging on the retina of our eyes. Such an image which is formed
by converging of rays at a point is called a real image. The real image can be
obtained on a screen (in the example of ceiling fan, the screen is the retina of
our eyes). To conclude:
A real image is formed by the actual intersection of the rays (reflected or
refracted) of light at a point. This image can be seen if a screen is placed at
that point. A real image is formed in front of a mirror.
On the other hand, an image which is formed at a point from where the
reflected (or refracted) light rays appear to diverge is called a virtual image.
A virtual image cannot be projected on a screen. A virtual image is formed
behind a mirror. For example, the image of your face made by a plane mirror is
a virtual image. You cannot project that image on a screen. In fact, you see your
face behind the mirror. If you place a screen behind the mirror, then no face will
be projected on it. The reason is that the rays do not actually meet there.
We will be able to understand the concept of virtual image in a better way
by learning the image formation of a point object by a plane mirror.
9. IMAGE FORMATION OF A POINT OBJECT BY A PLANE
MIRROR
To find the image of point object 0 placed in front of a plane mirror MM', we
draw two rays starting from O, These rays fall on the mirror at N and N’ and
are reflected. The reflected rays NR and N’R’ are diverging, i.e. these reflected
rays will never actually meet. But if we produce the reflected rays backwards
with the help of dotted lines, these rays appear to meet at I. It seems as though
the reflected rays originate from I. This point I is the virtual image of the point
object O.
Therefore, we see that a virtual image
(a) is formed when the reflected rays are diverging, i.e. the reflected rays
do not actually meet. The virtual image can be located by producing the
reflected rays backwards.
