Based on the concept of focus and converging power of a concave mirror.
Hold a concave mirror such that its reflecting surface is towards the sun. Now,
orient the concave mirror such that the image of the sun forms on a sheet of
paper. You will observe a shining spot on the sheet of paper. This shining spot
Paper
is the image of the sun. If you increase or decrease the distance of the concave
shining spot
mirror from the sheet of paper, you will see that the brightness and the size of
image changes. At a particular distance the image is brightest and of very small
size. This is the focus of the concave mirror and the distance of this point from the
pole of the mirror is the focal length.
What will happen if you hold the paper in that position for some time? The paper will start burning
at the point of image formation. Why? Because the infra-red radiations from the sun has been converged

Step 2:

7.2. Uses of Concave Mirrors
Concave mirrors (and parabolic mirrors) are used to concentrate sunlight
to generate high temperature in solar furnaces.
2. Concave mirror is used as a shaving mirror because it shows a magnified
and erect image of your face when your face is between the pole and
focus of the mirror. These are also used by dentist to see an enlarged
image of teeth.
3. Concave mirrors are used as reflectors in torches, car head-lights, search-
light to guide the powerful rays to longer distances. It is also used by
ENT doctors to focus light in the ear or nose.

Based on position and nature of images formed by a concave
mirror for different positions of object.
Fix a concave mirror on an optical stand which has a metre
scale and two trolley on rails attached to it in horizontal direction.
Place a lighted candle on one trolley and attach a screen on the
other trolley. In the first position the candle trolley is far from
the mirror. You will see that you get the sharpest image of the
candle on screen when the screen trolley is at the focus of the
concave mirror.
Now, move the candle trolley towards the mirror. You will
F
notice that to get the sharpest image of the candle on the screen,
you will have to move the screen trolley away from the mirror. Also, the image is real and inverted and
its size increases. You can also find the position of candle and its image.
When the candle trolley and the screen trolley are at a particular position on the scale the size of the
image of candle on the screen is equal to that of the candle. This is the point C. At this point the location of
the object and the image is same. When you bring the candle trolley very near to the pole (between P and F)
you won't be able to find the image on the screen. This is because now the image formed is virtual and
cannot be brought on the screen. You can see the image in the mirror.

Based on image formation by convex mirror.
Place two trolleys on the rails of an optical bench. On one trolley fix a
convex mirror such thatits reflecting surfaceis towards the other trolley.
Fix a pen on the other trolley. Place the two trolleys as close as possible.
You will see a virtual and erect image of the pen when you watch the
reflecting surface of the mirror. The image will appear behind the
mirror. Now move the trolley (on which the penis attached) away from
the trolley on which the mirror is fixed. Simultaneously see the reflecting surface of the mirror to watch the
image. You will find that the image remain virtual and erect but decreases in size and it moves away from
the mirror towards the focus of the mirror.
Conclusion. When the object moves away from the convex mirror, the image also moves from the convex
mirror towards its focus and simultaneously its size decreases. The image remain virtual and erect throughout.

22. HOW TO DISTINGUISH BETWEEN A PLANE MIRROR,
CONCAVE MIRROR AND CONVEX MIRROR WITHOUT
TOUCHING THEM
Bring your face close to the mirror and see the image of your face.
(a) If the image of face is of same size, the mirror is a plane mirror.
(b) If the image of face is magnified, the mirror is a concave mirror.
(c) If the image of face is diminished, the mirror is a convex mirror.
It is because of this that we use convex mirror as a rear view mirror. For the same reason, a full length
image of a tall tree or a tall building can be seen in a convex mirror and not plane or concave mirror.
yy
Based on images formed by concave and convex mirror.
The inner side of the spoon acts as a concave mirror. When you view
the image of your face keeping your face close to the spoon, you get a
virtual, erect and enlarged image. As you move the spoon slowly away
from your face, image becomes real and inverted and highly enlarged.
As the distance between the spoon and your face goes on increasing the
size of the image diminishes but the image remains real and inverted
(Refer Table 7.7).
The outer side of the spoon acts as a convex mirror. When you view
the image of your face keeping your face close to the spoon, you get
a virtual, erect and diminished image. As you move the spoon slowly
away from your face, image size diminishes and the image remains
Quiside BOW
Inside Bowl
virtual and erect (Refer Table 7.2).
Conclusion. The above activity depicts the type of images formed by a concave and convex mirror
when the object is placed at different positions from the mirror.

Ray Diagrams for the Formation of Images for Different Positions of Objects
Methodology
Step i:
Place an object AB perpendicularly on the principal axis of the convex
lens.
Step 2:
Draw two rays starting from the tip of the object (B). For convenience
use the above rules.
Step 3:
(a) Ifthe rays are converging, then you get the image of the tip of the
object at the point where the rays meet (B’). You get a real image.
(b) If the rays are diverging, then produce the rays backwards by
dotted lines. The image of the tip is the point where the dotted
lines meet (B’). This is a virtual image.
Step 4:
Drop a perpendicular from the point of image on the principal axis.
This is the final image of the object.

38. POWER OF COMBINATION OF THIN LENSES IN CONTACT
When a number of thin lenses are placed in direct contact with each other, the
power of the combination of lenses is equal to the algebraic sum of the powers of
individual lenses.
Power of the combination,
N
= P_1 + P_2 + ...
where P_1, P_2... are the powers of the individual lenses.
The use of combination of lenses are:
(a) To increase the magnification.
(b) To reduce certain defects caused due to the use of a single lens, such as
chromatic aberration.
Itisimportant tonote thatusing the term 'power' simplifies the mathematical
calculation as compared to the use of focal lengths by the formula.

called a concave mirror. A spherical mirror which has reflecting surface away from the centre of sphere, of
which the mirror is a part, is called convex mirror.

after reflection converges.
Focus of a convex mirror is a point on the principal axis from which a beam of light parallel to principal axis
after reflection appears to diverge.

A convex lens is made up of a transparent medium bounded by two spherical surfaces such that it is thick at the
middle and thin at the edges.
A concave lens is made up of a transparent medium bounded by two spherical surfaces such that it is thin at the
middle and thick at the edges.
A straight line passing through the centres of curvature of the two surfaces of a lens is called the principal axis.
There is a point on the principal axis in the lens, a ray of light passing through which, passes through the lens
undeviated. This point is called optical centre.
The principal focus of a converging lens is the point to which a beam of light parallel to the principal axis after
refraction converges.
The principal focus of a diverging lens is the point from which a beam of light parallel to the principal axis after
refraction appears to diverge.

a magnified virtual as well as real image. Is this
a correct statement? If yes, where shall the object
be placed in each case for obtaining these images?

For magnified virtual image : Object should be

between the F and 2F i.e., between 20 cm and 40 cm
from the lens.
Sudha finds out that the sharp image of the
window pane of her science laboratory is formed
at a distance of 5 cm from the lens. She now
tries to focus the building visible to her outside
the window instead of the window pane without
disturbing the lens. In which direction will she
move the screen to obtain a sharp image of the
building? What is the approximate focal length
of this lens?
When an object placed beyond 2F from a convex
lens is taken away from the lens, the image shifts
nearer to the lens. Therefore, in order to see distinct
image of the building, Sudha should move the
screen nearer to the lens. The approximate focal
length is 5 cm.

Radius is perpendicular to a point on the sphere.

point with the centre of curvature.
A ray of light passing through the centre of
curvature of a concave mirror retraces its path.

This is according to law of reflection. When a ray
of light passes through the centre of curvature it strikes
the mirror normally. Therefore, angle of incidence is
zero and angle of reflection is also zero.
Why is concave mirror used by doctors?
This is because it converges a parallel beam of
light incident on it at a point. Because of this the
intensity of light is increased at that point, and ear,
throat, nasal passage, teeth can be examined easily.

The concepts of optics studied so far are useful in designing many (
optical instruments such as microscope, telescope, camera, binoculars,
periscope, etc. A natural optical device is
a human eye. First we will
study human eye, the defects of vision and their remedial measures. In
the last section we will focus on colours of light, twinkling of stars, etc.
HUMAN EYE
.7. Construction
Human eye is almost spherical in shape having a diameter of
approximately 2.3 cm.

Fig. . Human eye
The front portion which sharply bulges out is covered with a
transparent and tough membrane called cornea. Behind the cornea
is a region which contains a liquid called aqueous humour. Next to it
is present a circular coloured diaphragm called iris with a hole in its
centre called pupil.
Behind iris is a crystalline convex lens held in its place by ciliary
muscles. After the lens, the eye is composed of vitreous humour. The
image is formed on a delicate inner-most light-sensitive membrane of the
eye called retina. Retina contains a blind spot where the optic nerve enters
the eye. It is called blind spot because it is totally insensitive to light.
1.2. Function of Iris and Pupil The function of iris is to regulate the amount of light entering the eye.
The function of iris is to regulate amount of light entering an
eye by changing the size of pupil by an involuntary muscle control.

When the intensity of light entering the eye is high, the pupil
contracts so as to reduce the amount of light entering the eye
and vice-versa. The pupil takes some time to adjust its size. You
must have experienced that while entering a cinema hall, it is
difficult to locate your seat. But after some time you are able to
see the other persons sitting in the hall. This happens because
when you were out of the cinema hall where intensity of light
was high, the size of the pupil was small. When you entered the
cinema hall where the intensity of light is low, the size of the
pupil is insufficient to bring in the required amount of light. By
involuntary muscle control the size of pupil increases. Therefore,
after some time you are able to see the other persons sitting in
the hall.

Retina is a screen of eye
on which light falls and a
real image is formed.
The light rays entering the eye are focussed on the retina by the eye lens. A
real and inverted image of the object is produced on the retina. It is important
to note that most of the refraction of light entering the eye is done by the
cornea. Only the final focussing is done by the eye lens. The retina converts
light energy into electrical energy. The electrical signals produced by the retina
reaches the brain by optic nerves. The brain interprets the electrical signals and
produces sensation of vision. If retina or optic nerve gets damaged it leads to
visual impairment.

The near point is at a distance of 25 cm and this distance is called least
distance of distinct vision, represented by D.
4. DEFECTS OF VISION
Weakening of ciliary muscles, change in the size of eye ball, irregularities
on the surface of cornea, formation of hazy membrane over the eye-lens,
etc. give rise to a number of defects of vision. Let us study these defects.
4.7. Myopia
(short-sightedness)
Myopia is a defect in which a human eye can see nearby objects distinctly
but is unable to see distant objects distinctly.
A myopic eye can see near by objects clearly, but is unable
to see distant object clearly. This is because rays coming from
infinity are converged before retina (see Fig 4 (b). The far point
which should be infinity has come closer and is at a distance
'x’ from eye, see Fig 4(a). This is shown by point 'F'. This point
is generally a few metres from the eye. It is because of this
reason that students suffering from myopia are unable to read
writing on black board from back benches.
Fe.
The reasons for myopia are:
(a) High converging power of eye-lens because ciliary
muscles do not relax sufficiently.
(b) Eye ball being longer than normal because of which
the distance between eye-lens and retina increases.
Correction: This defect is corrected by placing a
concave lens before the eye. The parallel rays coming from
distant object is first diverged by the concave lens and then
converged by the eye-lens. The power of concave lens is chosen
such that it creates only that much divergence so that after the
converging action of eye-lens the image is formed on the retina.

5.
CATARACT
The eye lens is made up of proteins arranged in a regular pattern. Because
of this regular arrangement the eye-lens is transparent. In some eyes,
the regular pattern gets disturbed and this decreases the transparency
of the eye-lens. If the arrangement disturbs to a greater extent it may
lead to an opaque eye-lens. This is called cataract. This defect is usually
found in old age.
Correction: This defect cannot be corrected by placing a suitable lens
before the eye-lens. Instead, it is corrected by a surgical operation by
replacing the affected lens by an artificial lens.
EYE DONATION
You must have seen advertisment in media persuading for eye
donation. If cornea of the eyes are removed within 6 hours of the death
of a person, it can be transplanted to a person suffering from corneal
blindness. There are more than 45 lakh cases of corneal blindness and
unfortunately out of these a major portion is that of children aged
below 2 years. If a person comes forward for eye donation, he can
save two corneal blind people by donating one eye to each. What one
has to do is go to an eye-bank, fill up the form giving his/her consent
for eye donation. On his/her death, the eye-bank is informed. Persons
from the eye-bank will come home (or in hospital) and remove the
cornea. It takes l0-5 minutes for the removal. The eye taken by the
eye-bank is checked thoroughly for any defect. If found defective it is
Persons who wear spectacles can donate eyes. Even persons having
hypertension, diabetes, etc. can donate eyes. Age is not a bar for eye
donation. But persons who are infected by AIDS, Hepatities B or C,
rabies, acute leukaemia, encephalitis, tetanus cannot donate eyes.
An eye-bank has strict standards to keep the identities of the donor
and recipient confidential. How exciting it feels to think that after one’s
death, she (or he) can make two blind persons see this wonderful world!

Stars are very far away and thus act as a point source of light. Light

is nearer as compared to stars. Therefore, a planet appears bigger as well. It
cannot be treated as a point source of light. In fact, a planet can be considered
as a collection of large number of point sources. If intensity of light from one
point source decreases, it increases from the other such that the overall average
remains the same. Therefore, planets do not twinkle.

The front part of eye that sharply bulges out which is covered with transparent

Circular coloured diaphragm present in eye.

Ahole in iris.

Changes the focal length of eye lens.
Far point

unable to see distant objects distinctly.

The phenomenon of splitting up of white light into constituent colours.

directions.

e

is called cataract. This can be corrected by replacing the affected lens by an artificial lens.

Dispersion of light occurs because the speed of light in a medium is different for different wavelengths.
When two identical prisms are placed parallel to each other in upside down position with each other, light coming
out of the combination of prisms is white light. This phenomenon is called recombination of spectrum colour.

Rainbow is seen due to dispersion produced by water droplets present in clouds on a rainy day.

The sunlight while travelling from the earth’s atmosphere scatters blue light more than red. Therefore, sky looks
blue.

at the sun is red.
Clouds look white because water droplets present in the sun scatter all wavelengths due to their large size.
Combination of all colours of light gives white light.

What happens to the image distance in the eye
when we increase the distance of object from the
eye?
(CBSE 2008)
The image distance remains the same as the
distance between eye-lens and retina remains
same. The focal length of eye-lens changes when
the object distance changes.
Why do stars twinkle?
(CBSE 2075)
The light from stars reaches us after atmospheric
refraction. The atmosphere is not steady because
of the changes in temperature and air mobility.
Therefore, the refractive index of air in a given
region keeps on changing continuously and
randomly. Due to this the amount of light reaching
us is not always the same. Therefore, stars appear
twinkling.
Explain why planets do not twinkle. (CBSE 2075)
Stars are very far away and thus act as a point
source of light. Light coming from a point source
is effected by the atmospheric changes. A planet
is nearer as compared to stars. Therefore, a planet
appears bigger as well. It cannot be treated as
a point source of light. In fact, a planet can be
considered as a collection of large number of point
sources. If intensity of light from one point source
decreases, it increases from the other such that
the overall average remains the same. Therefore,
planets do not twinkle.
Why does the sun appear reddish early in the
morning ?
(CBSE 2072)
During sunset (and sunrise) sunlight travels a
long distance through the earth’s atmosphere
before reaching the observer. Most of the blue
light is scattered. White light from which blue
light has been removed looks red. Therefore an
observer looking at sun during sunset (or sunrise)
experiences the colour of the sun as red.
Why does the sky appear dark instead of blue to
an astronaut ?
(CBSE 2074
This is because there is no atmosphere at such
height. On earth sky looks blue because of scattering
of light. If there would have been no atmosphere
on earth, the sky would have appeared black from
earth also.

as well as distant objects is called the power of accomodation.
The image is formed on retina. The distance of retina is fixed from the eye lens. Therefore the distance of image
from the eye is constant. In fact the focal length of eye lens changes. When we see distant object, power of
converging is less because focal length of eye lens is large. And when we see object at least distance of distinct
vision, power of converging is more because focal length of eye lens is small.

object, the focal length is small and the curvature is large.

Myopia is one type of refractive errors, which can be defined as a state in which the rays of the light of an object
are brought to focus in front of the retina. It is also
called nearsightedness, in which the eye fails to see
distant object properly. The most common surgery to
correct myopia is LASIK. An examiner laser is used
to reshape (flatten) the cornea, shifting the focus. The
other way out is to use a corrective lens before the
defective eye. The population suffering from myopia
in India in 202 was just over 28% and is expected
to rise to 34% by 2020 and approximately 50% in
2050, which is a major concern. According to a study
done by AIIMS, 7% children or
out of 6 children
aged between 5-[5 years are suffering from myopia.
According to UN data, countries where myopia
prevalence was estimated and measured as low in
the past, such as India, will have major increases by 2050. Myopia is rising in severity and being diagnosed at a
very early age amongst school going children. The risk factors can be genetic many times. Supposedly for a child
who has either or both parents suffering from myopia, the risk increases by three times in case of one of them
and by 6 times if both the parents are already suffering from it. But this is not the major cause. In the present
time youngster have started being hooked indoors to their phones, computers and tablets. Outdoor activities
have reduced considerably as a result. Also, being engaged with extra-curricular activities, homework and being
focused on studies further reduces the outdoor time. Eyes require critical visual simulation. This is only achieved
when children play outside or are engaged in outdoor activities because when they look at distant objects only
when they are outdoors.
(i) The eye defect in which a human eye can see nearby objects distinctly but is unable to see clearly distant objects
is called
|
(a) myopia
(b) hypermetropia
Normal vision a)
Focal plane
(c) cataract
(वर) presbyopia
